title.en: A secret that sounds too good to be true

text.en: Suppose someone told you that a few drops of a special liquid could turn a spoon into gold. Would you spend years chasing it? In this story by Sudha Murty, a man does exactly that, and the way the tale ends teaches a lesson that every student can use. Let us read it like a detective, looking for what really makes the gold appear.

This is the first story of Unit 1, called Fables and Folk Tales. A fable or folk tale is a short story that carries a lesson about life. Before reading, the book asks you to match four words with pictures: worried, plantation, sage and surprise. A plantation is a large farm with one kind of crop, and a sage is a wise and respected old person. It also asks you to remember a time when you worked hard, how it helped you and how it made you feel. Keep that memory in mind, because the story is about the value of hard work.
Rama Natha was the son of a rich landlord and was left large areas of land when his father died. But he never looked after the land. He believed that somewhere a magic potion existed that could turn any object into gold, and he spent all his days learning about it. People kept cheating him by promising to share the secret, yet he never gave up. His wife Madhumati was tired of this and also worried, because the family money was being wasted and soon they might have nothing.
One day a famous sage named Mahipati came to the town, and Rama Natha became his follower and asked about the potion. To his surprise the sage said yes, he had heard in the Himalayas how it could be made, but it was difficult. The sage set the conditions. Rama Natha must plant a banana plant, water it himself, and collect the morning dew from its leaves in winter. When he had five litres of dew, the sage would chant magic words to turn it into the potion, and one drop would change any object into gold. Rama Natha worried that winter lasts only a few months. The sage said he could plant as many banana plants as he liked, but he must look after them himself and collect the dew with his own hands.
Rama Natha went home and started clearing his big fields, which had been empty for years. He planted row after row of banana plants and took care of them with great attention. In the winter months he collected the dew from the leaves carefully. His wife helped him, and Madhumati also gathered the bananas, took them to the market and sold them for a good price. Each year he planted more, until he had a huge plantation. At the end of six years he finally had his five litres of dew.
Rama Natha carried the bottle to the sage. The sage smiled, muttered something over it and gave it back, telling him to try it. Rama Natha sprinkled a few drops on a copper vessel and waited. Nothing happened. He angrily said the sage had cheated him and wasted six precious years. The sage called Madhumati, who came with a big box. When she opened it, it was full of stacks of gold coins. The sage explained that no such potion exists. The wealth came from Rama Natha working on the land while his wife sold the fruit in the market. If the sage had said this earlier, Rama Natha would not have listened, so the sage played a trick. Rama Natha understood the wisdom in those words and from that day he worked even harder on his plantation.
The main message is that hard work, not magic or shortcuts, creates wealth and happiness. Look at how the characters change. Before meeting the sage, Rama Natha chased a dream and wasted his time and money. After the sage, he looked after his land and earned honestly. Notice also that Madhumati is a quiet hero. She worried, helped in the fields and sold the fruit, so the family gold was the result of teamwork. Another small lesson is that the sage used patience and a clever plan, because a lecture would not have changed Rama Natha. Experience taught him better than advice.
The book gives these story words: promised, remember, spending, huge, cheated, difficult, luck and market. Using them in your own sentences is the best way to own them. Words from the story such as potion, sage, dew, chant, tended, muttered, precious and wisdom each have a clear meaning. Tended means looked after, muttered means spoke in a low voice, and precious means very valuable. Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings. Examples are dew and due, son and sun, ate and eight, see and sea, and I and eye. Notice the pair your and you're. Your shows that something belongs to you, while you're is the short form of you are. Practice sentence: I ate eight bananas for breakfast. It uses the pair ate and eight correctly.
The book teaches joining sentences with words such as when, because, before and as soon as. Because gives a reason, before and as soon as show time. For example, the children ran towards the gate as soon as the bell rang. Here the bell ringing is the time of the action. He did not want to try rock climbing because of his fear of heights. Here the fear is the reason. The letter s can sound like /s/ as in sage or like /z/ as in trees or wisdom. In surprise, the first s is /s/ and the second is /z/. To speak well about hard work, use signal phrases: firstly, secondly, lastly, or to begin with, next, finally. They make your ideas easy to follow.

problem.en: Put the events in order: A the sage smiled; B Rama Natha gave the bottle to the sage; C Rama Natha dropped a few drops on a copper vessel; D the sage said words in a low voice over the water; E Rama Natha waited to see if the magic worked.

text.en: Start with B: Rama Natha must hand over the bottle first.

why.en: Nothing can happen to the water until the sage has the bottle.

text.en: Then A and D: the sage smiled and muttered over the water.

why.en: The sage acts on the water after receiving it.

text.en: Then C: the bottle is returned and Rama Natha sprinkles drops on the copper vessel.

why.en: He can only try it after the sage gives it back.

text.en: Last is E: he waits to see gold, but nothing happens. The order is B, A, D, C, E.

why.en: Waiting comes after the drops are sprinkled.

problem.en: Complete with a word from the story: Seeing that the plant had dried up, the gardener ____ some water on it.

text.en: Check the tense: the gardener acted in the past, so we need a past-tense verb.

why.en: The sentence says had dried up, which is past.

text.en: The story word that fits is sprinkled, so the sentence reads: the gardener sprinkled some water on it.

why.en: Rama Natha sprinkled a few drops on a copper vessel in the same way.

problem.en: Write a sentence using the homophones ate and eight.

text.en: Check meanings: ate is the past tense of eat, and eight is the number 8.
Use both in one sentence: I ate eight bananas at breakfast.

why.en: The sentence is meaningful and spells both correctly.

prompt.en: Explain in your own words why Rama Natha never became rich by magic but still got gold.

requiredIdeas.en: The gold came from Rama Natha planting and caring for banana plants and Madhumati selling the bananas.
Hard work over six years created the wealth.
The sage played a trick so Rama Natha would learn this himself.

commonMisconceptions.en: The sage really had a magic potion that failed.

points.en: A Bottle of Dew is a fable by Sudha Murty in Unit 1, Fables and Folk Tales.
Rama Natha believed in a magic potion that turns objects into gold.
The sage asked him to plant banana plants and collect dew for five litres, which took six years.
The gold coins came from hard work and from Madhumati selling the bananas.
Homophones sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning, for example dew and due, ate and eight.
Linking words like because, before and as soon as join ideas by reason and time.
